title: Is one Durable Object per topic the right shape, and what does the whole Cloudflare stack cost at 100 / 10k / 1M users?
summary: The brief's hypothesis. Answer with limits and prices from developers.cloudflare.com, dated, not from memory; and with the alternative shapes (DO per channel, D1-first, R2 event logs) weighed on scale, cost, isolation, concurrency, persistence, complexity, failure modes, migration, security.

title: run_worker_first, ASSETS binding and not_found_handling let one Worker serve dynamic routes over static assets
summary: Default (run_worker_first false): assets are served without invoking the Worker. Set run_worker_first true (or an array like ["/api/*","!/api/docs/*"]) to unconditionally run the Worker first for matching routes. env.ASSETS.fetch(request) lets the Worker fetch a static asset programmatically by pathname (hostname ignored). not_found_handling = "single-page-application" is what this repo already sets. So one Worker can run /api/* dynamically and fall through to static HTML for everything else, in one project.

title: Worker CPU, subrequest and body-size limits by plan (fetched 2026-09-04)
summary: CPU time per request: Free 10ms, Paid 30s default (configurable to 5 min). Subrequests per invocation: Free 50, Paid 10,000 (up to 1M with Smart Placement disabled or 10M via limits.cpu_ms style config per docs). Request body size: Free/Pro 100MB, Business 200MB, Enterprise up to 5GB self-serve. Worker scripts per account: Free 100, Paid 500. Env vars: 64/Worker (Free), 128/Worker (Paid), 5KB each.

title: Workers Cache API (cache.put/cache.match) does not honor stale-while-revalidate; the zone-level edge cache does
summary: Cloudflare docs, quoted directly: stale-while-revalidate is not supported when using the Cache API methods cache.match or cache.put. The zone-level HTTP cache (driven by Cache-Control response headers, no Worker code) does support it and now serves stale content immediately while revalidating in the background (UPDATING status). So a Worker wanting SWR semantics for its own dynamic JSON must fake it with KV or a manual background fetch, not the Cache API alone.

title: Durable Objects pricing unchanged as of 2026-09-04: 0.15 dollars per million requests, 12.50 per million GB-s
summary: Pricing page last-updated 2026-08-25, matches the 2026-08-30 figures already in imagine/stream/doc/durable-objects.md. Paid: 1M requests/mo included then 0.15 dollars/M; 400,000 GB-s/mo included then 12.50 dollars/M GB-s. SQLite storage billing (effective January 2026): 25B rows read/mo included then 0.001 dollars/M, 50M rows written/mo included then 1.00 dollar/M, 5GB-mo storage included then 0.20 dollars/GB-mo. Free plan: 100k requests/day, 13,000 GB-s/day, 5GB total storage, SQLite-backed classes only.

title: A single Durable Object handles roughly 500 to 1,000 requests per second before overload; this is the hot-object ceiling
summary: The limits page states an individual object has a soft limit of 1,000 requests per second before returning overloaded errors. Cloudflare best-practices guidance (rules-of-durable-objects) gives the same range explicitly: approximately 500-1,000 requests per second for simple operations, and names a global-singleton DO handling all traffic as the documented anti-pattern, recommending natural coordination boundaries (per user, per room, per document) instead.

title: The 32,768 WebSocket-connections-per-object figure is not on the current limits page; no official cap could be found today
summary: imagine/stream/doc/durable-objects.md cites 32,768 as a per-object WebSocket cap with a flag that it is not on the limits page and may be stale. Re-fetching the limits page on 2026-09-04 found a 32 MiB per-message size limit stated, but no explicit maximum concurrent WebSocket connections per object. The docs own caveat (CPU and memory usage may further limit the practical number) suggests this was never a hard published ceiling. Treat any specific connections-per-object number as unverified until Cloudflare states one.

title: Durable Objects: 10GB storage per object, 2MB max row/blob, 500 classes per account on Paid
summary: From the limits page, fetched 2026-09-04: storage per object 10GB on Workers Paid (SQLite-backed); key/value or SQL row/string/BLOB capped at 2MB; CPU time 30s default, configurable to 5 minutes active CPU via limits.cpu_ms; unlimited objects per account/class; 500 DO classes per account on Paid, 100 on Free. Free-plan total storage is capped at 5GB across all objects (footnote), which is the real free-tier ceiling, not a per-object one.

title: One DO per topic works at 100-10k users; the failure mode is a single hot topic hitting the per-object request ceiling
summary: At 100 users and even 100 topics, one DO per topic is free: each object handles a handful of req/s, well inside the free 100k requests / 13,000 GB-s daily. At 10k users over 500 topics, average load per DO stays low and cost is dominated by the Workers Paid base plus modest overage, tens of dollars a month. The failure mode is concentration, not scale: one viral topic pulling a large share of 1M users through a single object hits the 500-1,000 req/s soft ceiling long before account-wide totals do, since the cost model is per-account but the hot-object limit is per-object. The fix in Cloudflare own best-practices is sharding a hot key into multiple objects, undesigned here.

title: No documented pattern exists for detecting a hot topic and re-sharding its Durable Object at runtime
summary: Cloudflare docs describe sharding as a design-time choice (pick a sharding key up front) not a runtime rebalancing operation. Nothing found describes moving an existing hot objects state into N new shard objects without an application-level migration (read old object, fan writes into new ones, redirect routing). For a topic that goes viral after launch, this would be manual, and every client would need to learn the new shard key. This is the sharp edge of the one-DO-per-topic hypothesis and nobody has published a recipe for it.

title: D1 pricing 2026-09-04: 5GB storage and 5M rows read / 100k written per day free; overage priced per million rows
summary: Free (Workers Free): 5M rows read/day, 100k rows written/day, 5GB total storage. Paid (Workers Paid): 25 billion rows read/month included then 0.001 dollars/M; 50 million rows written/month included then 1.00 dollar/M; 5GB storage included then 0.75 dollars/GB-mo. No egress or throughput charges. Billing is scale-to-zero: nothing charged when the database is idle.

title: D1 limits: 10GB max database size (Paid, not raisable), 50,000 databases per account, 100KB max statement
summary: Free plan: 500MB per database, 10 databases, 5GB total account storage. Paid plan: 10GB per database (hard ceiling, cannot be increased even on request), 50,000 databases per account, 1TB total account storage. Query limits: 100,000-byte max SQL statement, 100 max bound parameters, 30s query timeout, up to 1,000 queries per Worker invocation on Paid (50 on Free). This shapes a database-per-topic pattern directly: 10GB is generous for text/metadata per topic but this is a hard wall, not a soft one.

title: D1 Sessions API gives sequential consistency across read replicas: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, no extra cost
summary: withSession() attaches a bookmark to each query identifying database state, startable unconstrained (any replica), primary-first (freshest data), or from a prior bookmark. This guarantees read-my-own-writes, monotonic reads and writes, and writes-follow-reads across replicas without global serialization. Billing is the same rows-read/written metering regardless of replica used; no premium for using it. Only reachable via the D1 Worker binding, not yet via the REST API.

title: D1 Time Travel gives free point-in-time restore: 30 days on Paid, 7 days on Free, no setup and no extra cost
summary: Time Travel is automatic; restoring uses wrangler d1 time-travel info to fetch a bookmark for a timestamp then wrangler d1 time-travel restore, which overwrites the live database in place (destructive). Retention: 30 days on Workers Paid, 7 days on Workers Free. Database history and restoring incur no additional cost. This is the same 30-day PITR window Durable Objects offer via getBookmarkForTime, so both storage primitives get free version history without building it.

title: D1 supports the SQLite FTS5 full-text-search extension natively, including fts5vocab
summary: D1 documentation lists FTS5 among its supported subset of SQLite extensions, alongside JSON functions and math functions. This means topic or post content can get relevance-ranked full-text search (FTS5 ships BM25 ranking) directly in D1 with no external search service, which matters for the D1-for-content alternative to one-DO-per-topic.

title: D1 has no cross-database joins; Cloudflare recommends database-per-tenant as horizontal scaling, not an anti-pattern
summary: D1 has no cross-database query or join. Cloudflare positions this as intentional: D1 is designed for horizontal scale-out across many smaller (up to 10GB) databases keyed per-user, per-tenant or per-entity, and any cross-cutting aggregate (in this platform case, total activity across topics) must be computed in application code by querying each database separately, or exported to a separate analytics store. This bears directly on the DO-per-topic-plus-D1-for-content alternative named in the brief: a D1-per-topic pattern inherits the same no-cross-topic-query limitation a DO-per-topic pattern already has.

title: Workers KV: free tier writes capped at 1,000 per day; paid is 5.00 dollars per million writes, 0.50 per million reads
summary: Free: 100,000 reads/day, 1,000 writes/day, 1,000 deletes/day, 1,000 list ops/day, 1GB stored. Paid (per month): 10M reads included then 0.50 dollars/M; 1M writes included then 5.00 dollars/M; 1M deletes included then 5.00 dollars/M; 1M list ops included then 5.00 dollars/M; 1GB storage included then 0.50 dollars/GB-mo. Eventual consistency window is roughly 60 seconds globally. The 1,000-write/day free cap and per-key billing rule out KV as a primary content store here; it fits config and published snapshots exactly as imagine/cms/services/page.js already concluded, never per-visitor writes.

title: R2 pricing: 0.015 dollars/GB-month storage, 4.50 dollars per million Class A ops, 0.36 per million Class B ops
summary: Standard storage: 0.015 dollars/GB-month (Infrequent Access 0.01). Class A (writes/lists): 4.50 dollars/M standard, 9.00 dollars/M Infrequent Access. Class B (reads): 0.36 dollars/M standard, 0.90 dollars/M Infrequent Access. Free tier: 10GB-month storage, 1M Class A ops/month, 10M Class B ops/month. Egress bandwidth is free in both classes, which is the headline feature versus S3. This makes R2 the natural home for JSONL event-log archives and media named in the brief: reads (serving media) are cheap Class B, writes (uploads, compaction) are the pricier Class A.

title: R2 presigned URLs need no Worker: AWS SigV4, 1 second to 7 days expiry, direct browser PUT uploads
summary: Presigned URLs are generated with R2 API credentials using AWS Signature Version 4, covering GET/PUT/HEAD/DELETE, with an expiry configurable from 1 second up to 604,800 seconds (7 days). No additional auth headers are required at request time, so a browser can PUT directly to R2 with only the URL, no Worker in the request path (a Worker or trusted backend is only needed to mint the URL, and to set CORS + ContentType restrictions on the bucket).

title: R2 event notifications (create/delete) push to Cloudflare Queues; consumer is a Worker or HTTP pull
summary: object-create fires on PutObject, CopyObject or CompleteMultipartUpload; object-delete fires on DeleteObject or lifecycle expiry. Messages carry account id, action, bucket, object key/size/eTag and timestamp, filterable by key prefix/suffix. Consumers are a Worker or an HTTP pull client; Queues per-queue throughput is 5,000 messages/second, so high-volume workloads need multiple queues. No R2-side notification fee is documented; cost is ordinary Queues billing.

title: R2 lifecycle rules: up to 1,000 per bucket; expire, transition to Infrequent Access, or abort multipart uploads
summary: Three actions: delete objects after N days or on a date (applied within about 24 hours of trigger); transition to Infrequent Access storage after N days (each transition costs one Class A op); abort incomplete multipart uploads after a set time (bucket default is 7 days). When rules conflict inside the same 24-hour window, deletion wins over class transition. Up to 1,000 rules per bucket. This is the mechanism for the brief JSONL-compaction-plus-cold-archive shape: keep hot JSONL in R2 Standard, transition compacted snapshots to Infrequent Access, expire raw logs after a retention window.

title: Queues: 1M ops/month free on Paid (10k/day on Free), then 0.40 dollars per million; one op is every 64KB
summary: Workers Free: 10,000 operations/day included. Workers Paid: 1,000,000 operations/month included, then 0.40 dollars/M. An operation is counted per 64KB chunk of a message written, read, or deleted (a 127KB message costs 2 operations for that step). A typical deliver-once message costs 3 operations (write, read, delete); retries add a read each. No egress or bandwidth charge. Message retention: 24 hours (Free), 4-14 days configurable (Paid).

title: Workflows added per-step and per-storage billing 2026-08-10: 3,000 steps/day free, 500,000/month on Paid
summary: Workflows share the Workers request and CPU-time SKUs (Free: 100,000 req/day shared with Workers, 10ms CPU/invocation; Paid: 10M requests/month then 0.30 dollars/M, 30M CPU-ms/month then 0.02 dollars/M-ms), and add step and storage dimensions effective 2026-08-10: Free 3,000 steps/day, 1GB storage; Paid 500,000 steps/month included then 0.80 dollars per additional 100,000, 1GB storage included then 0.20 dollars/GB-month. A Workflow paused on step.sleep or awaiting an API response does not accrue CPU time, so a long-running compaction/publish pipeline is cheap while waiting.

title: Cloudflare own docs disagree whether the cron-trigger limit (5 Free / 250 Paid) is per-Worker or per-account
summary: The Cron Triggers page tells readers to check Limits for the maximum number of Cron Triggers per Worker, but the Limits page itself labels the same numbers Number of Cron Triggers per account: 5 (Free), 250 (Paid). This is a live, unresolved documentation contradiction (open GitHub issue cloudflare/cloudflare-docs #29326, with an open but unmerged fix PR #32717). Practically: assume the account-level reading (5 total triggers on Free) is the safe one to design against, since it is the more restrictive interpretation and is what the Limits table literally says.

title: wrangler dev runs locally on workerd/Miniflare by default, no account needed; --remote uploads to a live preview
summary: Default local mode runs the Worker on the same workerd runtime used in production via Miniflare, simulating bindings locally with no account or network required. --remote instead uploads the Worker to a temporary Cloudflare preview environment on every save and forces all bindings to connect to real remote resources (no local simulation); it is documented as noticeably slower due to the per-change upload/deploy step. Durable Objects specifically always run locally in dev and cannot be pointed at the cloud at all (confirmed 2026-08-30 in the existing durable-objects.md and unchanged today).

title: Local D1/DO/KV/R2 state lives in .wrangler/state and persists by default; --persist-to relocates it
summary: wrangler dev creates local resource state under .wrangler/state in the project directory, with subfolders per binding type (kv, r2, d1, do). This persists across dev-server restarts by default; delete the folder (or a subfolder) to reset it. --persist-to <dir> changes the location, and Cloudflare documentation explicitly warns it must also be passed to any other Wrangler command that reads or writes that local data, or state splits across two locations. Cloudflare also recommends adding the persistence folder to .gitignore.

title: vitest-pool-workers is superseded by vitest-plugin, which also runs fully local on Miniflare, no account needed
summary: Current Cloudflare testing docs point users of the older vitest-pool-workers package to migrate to the new vitest-plugin. The current integration runs tests fully-locally using Miniflare, meaning D1/DO/KV/R2 bindings under test are the same local simulations wrangler dev uses, with no Cloudflare account required for the test suite itself.

title: No official doc covers node server.js plus wrangler dev side by side; recommend two ports and a dev-only proxy
summary: Nothing found in Cloudflare docs discusses coexisting with a separate non-Workers local server (they assume wrangler dev is the whole local stack). Community guidance points at wrangler dev --port to move off the default 8787, and a getPlatformProxy() API for injecting Cloudflare bindings into a foreign Node dev server, but neither is a tested recipe for this repo shape. Best available recommendation, unverified end to end: run node server.js on port 80 as today and wrangler dev --port 8787 for the Worker, then have server.js proxy any /api/* request to localhost:8787 so one browser origin sees both.

title: Workers AI: 10,000 Neurons/day free forever, then 0.011 dollars per 1,000 Neurons on Workers Paid
summary: Neurons are a single normalized unit covering tokens, image tiles, steps and audio minutes across model types. Free allocation resets daily at 00:00 UTC; beyond it requires Workers Paid at 0.011 dollars per 1,000 Neurons. Relevant only if this platform adds AI features (summarization, moderation, embeddings for search); not otherwise part of the core topic/DO/D1/R2 stack.

title: Cloudflare Realtime (WebRTC, formerly Calls): 1TB free egress/month then about 0.05 dollars/GB
summary: Community-sourced (not independently fetched from a pricing page today): 1TB free monthly egress, then approximately 0.05 dollars/GB for data Cloudflare sends to clients; ingress to Cloudflare is free; does not require Workers Paid. This is a WebRTC media relay, a different tool than the WebSocket-over-Durable-Object pattern already chosen for topic text/JSON sync; only relevant if the platform adds voice/video rooms.

title: Cloudflare Stream: about 1 dollar per 1,000 minutes delivered, 5 dollars per 1,000 minutes stored/month
summary: Search-sourced figures, not independently verified against an official pricing page today (fetch attempts on adjacent pages were blocked/404): delivery around 0.001 dollars per minute (1 dollar/1,000 min), storage around 5 dollars per 1,000 stored minutes per month, no separate egress or per-request charge. Relevant only if the platform hosts its own video rather than embedding YouTube/Vimeo as public/imagine/feeds/video already does.

title: Turnstile (CAPTCHA replacement) is free and unlimited on every plan: unlimited sitekeys, unlimited challenges
summary: Cloudflare own announcement states Turnstile is free for everyone with no usage-based charge; the free plan supports up to 20 widgets (15 hostnames per widget) with unlimited verification requests. Only Enterprise (contact-sales pricing) adds more widgets/hostnames and longer analytics retention. This is the obvious, zero-cost answer to bot-gating a topic sign-up or write form.

title: Access free-plan seat count (widely quoted as 50) unconfirmed on any primary docs page today
summary: Repeated fetch attempts against Cloudflare One overview, FAQ and seat-management pages today found no explicit free-seat number; the seat-management page describes how seats work for an existing subscription but not free-tier limits. The widely-repeated 50-users figure remains third-party-sourced only, matching the exact gap already flagged in public/imagine/cms/thinking.md on 2026-08-30. Verify in the live dashboard before relying on it; not needed for this platform anyway since Access gates a whole site/app behind login, the opposite of a public topic platform.

title: Email Routing (receiving) is free and unlimited on every plan; outbound sending needs Paid, 3,000 free/month
summary: Inbound Email Routing (forwarding mail sent to your domain) is unlimited on both Workers Free and Paid. Outbound sending to arbitrary recipients requires Workers Paid: 3,000 emails/month included, then 0.35 dollars per 1,000. Sending to your own verified destination addresses is free on all plans and does not consume the quota. Useful for transactional mail (invite links, digest emails) if the platform ever needs it; not part of the core cost model today.

title: Wrangler bundles npm deps into a Worker by default via esbuild, no build step needed; --no-bundle is discouraged
summary: Wrangler has built-in support for importing npm-defined modules from package.json and bundles automatically on deploy, with no separate build command needed (dry-run --outdir can preview the bundle). --no-bundle disables this and is intended for code pre-processed by other tooling; the docs explicitly discourage it in most cases because minification and polyfill injection are lost. This confirms a Worker with npm dependencies is the path of least resistance, which cuts against a zero-dependency Worker unless deliberately chosen with --no-bundle.

title: Recommend the no-new-npm-dependency law bind the Worker too: --no-bundle plus plain ESM, matching notes/auth
summary: CLAUDE.md predates any Worker; nothing in it says whether Wrangler bundling counts as a build step for the API half of the deploy. notes/auth/readme.md already commits to this stance for its own design: package.json gains nothing, an auth library would be the fourth dependency and the first one running in production, WebCrypto plus the D1 binding cover the whole need. Recommendation: keep that precedent as the house rule for every future Worker (deploy --no-bundle, hand-written ESM, ask before adding any npm dependency to worker/); nothing researched here requires a bundled dependency to reach D1/DO/KV/R2/Queues, all reachable via plain bindings, fetch and WebCrypto.

title: Static is always cheaper is true for content, but any per-visitor write or live update needs a server, on any host
summary: Every product researched here (D1, DO, KV, R2, Queues) only gets billed when invoked; static assets alone are free at any volume on Cloudflare Workers plans and remain the right default for pages nobody edits. But the moment a topic accepts a write from a visitor who is not the owner, or two tabs need to see each other live, static hosting cannot do it at all, on any host. So static is always cheaper is correct and simultaneously not an argument against this stack: the comparison should be Worker+DO+D1 versus another server cost for the dynamic slice only, not against doing nothing.

title: D1 is needed only when a visitor must write, confirming the existing cms/thinking.md verdict for the topic platform
summary: public/imagine/cms/thinking.md already concluded D1 buys nothing over git files until a visitor who is not the owner writes something, because a browser cannot safely hold a D1-scoped token (the REST API is account-scoped and Cloudflare own tutorial puts a proxy Worker in front of it). Nothing found while researching D1 today changes that: pricing, limits, Sessions API and Time Travel are all about a Worker-mediated database, never one a browser touches directly. For the topic platform this means D1 or DO storage is the right reach exactly where two-way sync or visitor writes exist, and pure content stays git files as long as only the owner edits it.

title: The one alternative that could beat Cloudflare: a single long-lived VM with a WebSocket server plus SQLite
summary: A single VM (Fly.io, a VPS, Railway) running node server.js style code with an in-process WebSocket hub and SQLite gives one true single-threaded order per process, the same guarantee a Durable Object gives per object, without a new storage API, hibernation model or edge billing unit. It wins on debuggability and matches this repo own dev-server pattern. It loses on everything Cloudflare optimizes for: no free global low-latency placement, a deploy that can go down and needs its own uptime story, and it reintroduces the always-on server CLAUDE.md avoids for the static half. Verdict: not a real contender here, but the shape this repo already trusts for local dev.

title: HTMLRewriter can wrap env.ASSETS.fetch() output to inject dynamic content into a static HTML page at the edge
summary: HTMLRewriter attaches via .on(selector, handler).transform(response). The documented pattern is: fetch the static asset with env.ASSETS.fetch(request), then .transform() that Response through one or more element handlers, which may themselves be async and fetch from KV, D1 or a Durable Object before injecting markup. This confirms Q1: a single Worker route can serve a static page and rewrite live data into it in one response, no separate API call from the browser needed for above-the-fold dynamic content.

title: Skeptic pass: the 5 dollar Workers Paid base unlocks each product own larger included allowance; it is not one shared 5 dollar bucket
summary: Confirms and ties together the separate DO/D1/R2/KV pricing entries above: being on Workers Paid (5 dollars/month minimum) raises each product free-style allowance on its own axis (10M Worker requests, 1M DO requests plus 400,000 GB-s duration, 25B D1 rows read, 50M D1 rows written, and so on), each metered and billed independently past its own line. The 5 dollars is a subscription gate, not a shared spending pool, so a cost estimate must sum every product overage separately rather than assuming 5 dollars covers a blended usage budget.

title: Skeptic pass: what would falsify one-DO-per-topic — an official low WebSocket cap, or measured single-region latency for a global audience
summary: Two things would overturn the recommendation and neither is ruled out by anything found today. First, if Cloudflare ever publishes a hard per-object WebSocket connection cap well under a few thousand, a popular topic room would need sharding far sooner than the request-rate ceiling implies. Second, an object never moves after creation (noted in durable-objects.md), so a topic created in one region serves every later global reader from that region; nothing found here measures whether that latency is acceptable for a worldwide audience versus Cloudflare own multi-region products. Neither has been tested against real traffic.
